name: Single Market Emergency Instrument (IMERA)
evidence_rating: ex-ante only: unquantified forecasts; applies from May 2026 and never yet activated
summary: The instrument gives the EU powers to keep goods, services and people moving in a crisis and, as a last resort, to request information from firms or prioritise orders for crisis goods. The Commission's impact assessment described the benefits only in general terms and flagged costs for businesses. It has applied only since May 2026 and has not been activated, so there is no evidence on its effects.

indicators.objective: The LFS lists no quantified indicators: it promises a Commission evaluation five years after application and regular monitoring of the effect of free-movement measures, information requests and strategic reserves
Minimise obstacles to free movement in crises
indicators.indicator: Fewer and better-coordinated national crisis restrictions
indicators.evidence: Regulation applies from 29 May 2026; no vigilance or emergency mode activated and no data found.

indicators.objective: Safeguard availability of crisis-relevant goods and services
indicators.indicator: Availability of crisis-relevant products during emergencies
indicators.evidence: No crisis activation yet; not measured.

literature.citation: European Commission (2022), Impact Assessment accompanying the Single Market Emergency Instrument proposal (executive summary SWD(2022) 290), SWD(2022) 289
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the Single Market Emergency Instrument proposal (executive summary SWD(2022) 290)
literature.outcomes: free movement in crises; supply of crisis-relevant goods; business costs
literature.headline: Benefits described qualitatively (fewer obstacles to free movement, better availability of crisis goods); costs for firms from information requests, ramp-up obligations and priority-rated orders; SMEs could be hit by mandatory information requests; no headline monetised figures
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected better crisis coordination and supply of essential goods but did not put a figure on the benefits, and warned that information requests and priority orders could burden firms.
